title: The universe in Krishna's mouth
hookLine: little Krishna is caught eating dirt, and his mother looks in his mouth
carry: smaller than small, greater than great
tomorrow: an archer who sees only the bird
last: ONE GOD, THROUGH THE FORM YOU LOVE.

cards: In the village of Gokula, little Krishna's friends run to his mother, Yashoda: he's been eating dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, eyes wide, and says they're lying.
If you don't believe me, look in my mouth. So she says: open. He opens his mouth.

And inside, the Bhagavata says, Yashoda sees the whole universe: the sky and the directions, mountains, islands and oceans, wind and fire, the moon and the stars, and her own village, with herself standing in it.

teach.b: She's frightened, then amazed. Then, the story says, Krishna covers the vision with a mother's love, and she lifts him onto her lap as if nothing happened. A toddler you could carry on one hip, holding everything.

teach.h: SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.
teach.b: Hindu scripture has a phrase for this: smaller than the small, greater than the great.
The Katha Upanishad says it, and so does the Shvetashvatara, which you met a couple of weeks ago: the divine self, hidden in every heart, is both.
It's why a Hindu can bow to a thumb-sized murti, or a smooth black shaligram stone, and mean the Lord of the whole universe. Size was never the measure. Now Patanjali.
Sutra 1.40, in paraphrase: the yogi's mastery reaches from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude. Paramanu, the smallest atom.
Parama mahat, the greatest greatness. Vashikara, mastery.
The commentator Vyasa explains: a mind steadied through any of yesterday's doors can rest on the subtlest object without slipping, and on the vastest without scattering. Small doesn't make it fidget.
Huge doesn't make it lose its grip.
Many teachers read the two together: the divine is smaller than small and greater than great, and a practiced mind becomes able to hold both.
The little murti on the shelf and the night sky over the roof aren't two different subjects. The sutra is also a hinge.
The list of doors is done, and next comes what happens inside absorption itself, with a mind like a clear crystal.

how: Yashoda's vision is a favorite of Krishna's childhood stories, often retold around Janmashtami, and Hindus bow to small murtis and shaligram stones as the Lord of all; students of the Yoga Sutras treat 1.40 as the sign that the mind has been steadied.

o: control won by pushing every thought away
mastery: a mind that stays steady on anything
the very smallest particle of all matter

games.q: small and great: tap the pairs.
p: sees the universe in Krishna's mouth
mastery: a mind steady on anything

s: Yashoda saw the universe after Krishna was accused of eating dirt
she told him to open his mouth, and saw sky, oceans, mountains and her own village.
sutra 1.40 is about gaining power over physical objects
Vyasa reads it as the mind resting steadily on any object, subtle or vast.
'smaller than the small, greater than the great' is said of the self in the Upanishads
the Katha and the Shvetashvatara both say it.

games.q: someone says a little murti on a shelf is too small to be God. what does today's teaching say?
o: they're right: God needs a big temple.
the divine is smaller than small and greater than great; size was never the measure.
small murtis only hold a small part of God.
games.why: Yashoda saw the universe in a toddler's mouth, and the Upanishads call the self smaller than the small, greater than the great.

practice: Rest your attention on the smallest thing you can feel, a fingertip on your knee, then widen to the whole body, the room, the sky over the roof, and come back to the fingertip.
If you pray, picture the form of God you love, small enough to sit in your palm, then as wide as the sky. Notice whether the steadiness holds as the size changes.

wordCard.voice: Vashikara, mastery, having it under control. Sutra 1.40: a steadied mind can rest on anything, from the tiniest particle to the greatest expanse, the way Yashoda found the universe in a toddler.

orig.note: Sanskrit vaśīkāra: mastery, bringing under control. the same word Patanjali uses for non-attachment's mastery in 1.15.

carryVoice: Your line: smaller than small, greater than great. A toddler's mouth, and the whole universe inside. Day four hundred forty-three, done.
